chunks: And by this chain, he said,
Abu Abdullah (peace be upon him) said: 'Only a believer is commanded to enjoin good and forbid evil, so he gives advice, or if ignorant, so he learns; and as for the owner of the whip or sword, no.'

key_terms.صَاحِبُ سَوْطٍ: Owner of the whip (symbol of force)
key_terms.صَاحِبُ سَيْفٍ: Owner of the sword (symbol of military force)

ai.seo_question: What is the difference between true admonition and physical coercion in Shia ethics?
ai.summary: Imam al-Sadiq (peace be upon him) clarifies that the command for 'enjoining good and forbidding evil' is directed specifically at the 'mu'min' (the knowledgeable believer) or the 'jahil' (the ignorant learner), emphasizing intellectual engagement over physical force. He explicitly excludes the 'sahib sawt' (holder of the whip) or 'sayf' (holder of the sword), critiquing the Umayyad and early Abbasid reliance on coercive power and military might as an invalid form of religious authority. This distinction underscores the Shia principle that true reform requires wisdom and teaching rather than brute coercion.

en.hubeali: ‘Abu Abdullah<sup>asws</sup> said: ‘But rather, a Believer would be enjoined with the good and forbid from the evil, so he would heed advice, or if ignorant, so he would learn, and as for the owner of the whip or a sword, so no!’.
en.sarwar: 2. It is narrated from the narrator of the previous Hadith who has said the following:
“Abu ‘Abd Allah, ‘Alayhi al-Salam, has said, ‘Only believing people who accept good advice should be asked to do good and prohibit committing evil but not those who have the whip and the sword.’”
